title: Fire and Rain on Mount Carmel
overview: After years of drought, Elijah challenges King Ahab and the prophets of Baal to a public test on Mount Carmel to show who is truly God, and then the rain returns.

parts.label: Elijah meets Obadiah (vv. 1-16)
parts.note: Obadiah ran King Ahab's palace but quietly worshiped the LORD, and he had risked his life hiding a hundred prophets from Queen Jezebel's killings. He is terrified that if he announces Elijah and the prophet vanishes again, the angry king will kill him instead.

parts.label: Who is troubling Israel? (vv. 17-21)
parts.note: Ahab blames Elijah for the drought, but Elijah blames the royal family for worshiping Baal, the Canaanite storm god people believed sent the rain. Elijah asks the people how long they will waver between the two, picturing someone limping back and forth between two paths.

parts.label: Baal's prophets cry out (vv. 22-29)
parts.note: Because Baal was worshiped as a god of storms, many readers think fire from the sky was a test on his own ground. His prophets shout, dance and cut themselves until they bleed, which the text simply calls their custom, while Elijah mocks the silence.

parts.label: Elijah's altar and the fire (vv. 30-39)
parts.note: The twelve stones stand for the twelve tribes, a reminder that Israel was meant to be one people under one God even though the kingdom had split. Elijah has the altar soaked with water, often read as showing no hidden fire was involved, and when fire burns up even the stones and the water, the crowd falls down and declares the LORD is God.

parts.label: Killing at the Kishon (v. 40)
parts.note: Elijah has the prophets of Baal seized and put to death at the brook below the mountain, and the chapter reports this without comment. Later interpreters often connect it to the death penalty in Israel's law for prophets of other gods, and many readers today find the scene deeply troubling.

parts.label: The rain returns (vv. 41-46)
parts.note: Elijah prays bent to the ground and sends his servant to look seven times until a cloud the size of a hand appears, and then a heavy storm ends the drought. Filled with the LORD's power, he tucks up his cloak and runs ahead of Ahab's chariot all the way to Jezreel, where the king had a palace.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the fire from heaven should be read mainly as a literal historical miracle or as a story shaped to make the point that the LORD, not Baal, rules over fire and rain.
think: When you have felt pulled between two ways of living or believing, what has kept you from settling on one?
